claims.text: Equiatomic FeNiCrMn has an FCC initial structure.
The initial FeNiCrMn material contains no pre-existing vacancy clusters or secondary phases.
Thermal vibrations reduce the critical resolved shear stress without causing spontaneous phase transformation under the proposed conditions.
Chemical short-range order and local lattice distortion in FeNiCrMn arise from atomic-size or lattice-parameter mismatch among its constituent elements.
Local lattice distortion creates a friction-like barrier to partial-dislocation motion.
The friction-like barrier hinders dislocation annihilation and thereby promotes high dislocation density.
The friction-like barrier can increase dislocation density without materially increasing the strain-rate sensitivity of macroscopic yield strength.
Dislocation nucleation in FeNiCrMn occurs by thermal activation over a local lattice-distortion barrier.
Vacancy clusters are not the governing dislocation-nucleation sites in the proposed FeNiCrMn material.
The <11-1> orientation requires a higher resolved stress for Shockley-partial nucleation than the <110> orientation.
The orientation dependence is caused by activation of a higher CRSS on the {111}<110> slip system for the <11-1> loading orientation.
The maximum yield stress is higher for <11-1>-oriented FeNiCrMn than for <110>-oriented FeNiCrMn.
Dislocation density increases as strain rate increases from 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1.
Yield strength remains relatively constant over strain rates from 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1.
The HCP-like regions are intrinsic stacking faults formed by separated Shockley partial dislocations.
The HCP-like regions are not products of a thermodynamic phase transformation.
A continuous local lattice parameter consistent with the FCC matrix, rather than a discrete new HCP lattice parameter, would discriminate a stacking fault from a true transformed phase.
At strain rates below 10^6 s^-1, dislocation annihilation is more efficient and yield strength is lower.
Some CoNiCrFeMn nanowires exhibit deformation twinning and FCC-to-HCP phase transformation.
Intentionally introduced vacancy clusters may become dislocation-nucleation sites and invalidate the proposed nucleation mechanism.
